title: Powering AI Through Grid-Positive Data Centers
gist: BCG argues power, not chips, is the decisive constraint on AI data-center buildout, with connection queues running 5-10 years, and proposes 'grid-positive' data centers that connect non-firm and lean on behind-the-meter generation/storage to energize years sooner without raising costs for other grid users. It focuses on Northwest Europe over 2030-2035 and models the least-cost mix of load flexibility, BTM assets, and firm vs. non-firm access.

themes.theme: Power as the binding constraint on AI

insights.claim: Leadership in AI is inseparable from the ability to build and power data centers, letting host economies capture significant value and a degree of technological sovereignty.
insights.speaker: Tom Brijs
insights.so_what: Treat national/regional power availability and connection policy as a leading indicator of where AI compute and its economic value will accrue.
insights.quote: The contest for leadership in AI is also a contest to build and power the data centers behind it, with the economies that host that compute capturing significant value and a measure of technological sovereignty.
insights.locator: The contest for leadership in AI

insights.claim: Global compute capacity is expected to more than double by 2030, requiring data-center connections at unprecedented scale and speed.
insights.speaker: Tom Brijs
insights.so_what: Sets the demand backdrop; grid interconnection capacity becomes the choke point that gates AI supply growth.
insights.quote: Global compute capacity is expected to more than double by 2030

insights.claim: Grid connection queues in many markets now run five to ten years, making power a decisive constraint on where and how fast data centers are built, alongside fiber, gas, cooling, and water.
insights.speaker: Tom Brijs
insights.so_what: Multi-year interconnection queues are a structural bottleneck; assets or policies that shortcut them command a scarcity premium.
insights.quote: connection queues in many markets now running five to ten years

themes.theme: Mobile AI workloads and locational competition

insights.claim: A growing share of AI workloads are not latency-sensitive, so the compute can locate wherever power is cheapest or can be secured first.
insights.speaker: Tom Brijs
insights.so_what: Capital chases the fastest, cheapest power; regions with slow interconnection risk losing mobile compute investment to faster rivals.
insights.quote: A growing share of AI workloads are not latency-sensitive, so the compute can locate wherever power is most competitive or can be secured first.
insights.locator: Much of this investment is also mobile

insights.claim: Connection speed has become a competitive lever between markets and regions vying for mobile AI investment.
insights.speaker: Tom Brijs
insights.so_what: Watch interconnection-reform policy as a differentiator; jurisdictions that speed connections can win compute share from slower neighbors.
insights.quote: Connection speed has therefore become a lever in the competition between markets and regions.
insights.locator: Much of this investment is also mobile

insights.claim: Whether a data center burdens or strengthens the electricity system is not predetermined but depends on how and where it connects and how it runs once online.
insights.speaker: Tom Brijs
insights.so_what: Reframes local opposition; the design and siting choices, not the load itself, determine net grid impact.
insights.quote: Whether a data center burdens or strengthens the system depends on how and where it connects, and how it runs once it is online.
insights.locator: Locally, though, data centers often face opposition

insights.claim: Load growth is a key lever for electricity affordability because it spreads fixed costs over more users, raises utilization, and lets demand materialize for the systems being expanded.
insights.speaker: Tom Brijs
insights.so_what: Counters the 'data centers raise everyone's bills' narrative; higher utilization can lower per-user costs if managed well.
insights.quote: load growth is a key lever for electricity affordability - spreading fixed costs over more users, raising utilization, and letting demand materialize
insights.locator: Although we firmly believe load growth

insights.claim: Data centers can come online years sooner without raising others' costs via two levers: connecting in a different place and/or non-firm (accepting curtailment during grid stress), and building the capability to shift flexible workloads and draw on behind-the-meter generation and storage.
insights.speaker: Tom Brijs
insights.so_what: Non-firm access plus BTM assets is the proposed route around 5-10 year queues; suppliers of BTM generation/storage and flexibility software are beneficiaries.
insights.quote: accept curtailment in the hours the grid is stressed, in exchange for skipping the years-long wait for firm grid capacity
insights.locator: It rests on two key levers

insights.claim: In congested Northwest European markets, achieving grid-positive outcomes will require data centers to host significant behind-the-meter capacity, adding to power supply costs.
insights.speaker: Tom Brijs
insights.so_what: Expect a structural build-out of on-site generation and storage at NW European data centers; a demand signal for BTM equipment vendors.
insights.quote: achieving this in already congested markets will require data centers to host significant BTM capacity
insights.locator: In Northwest Europe, the reality is

insights.claim: In BCG's studied cases, the value of energizing years sooner outweighs the added cost of hosting behind-the-meter capacity.
insights.speaker: Tom Brijs
insights.so_what: The speed-to-power premium can justify higher BTM spend; time-to-energization is the dominant value driver in the economics.
insights.quote: the value of energizing years sooner because of it outweighs this added cost
insights.locator: In Northwest Europe, the reality is

insights.claim: Under today's connection rules in many markets, data centers retain the right to wait for a firm connection wherever they site, with non-firm access merely optional.
insights.speaker: Tom Brijs
insights.so_what: Current rules preserve the incumbent firm-connection default; without reform the grid-positive model won't be adopted at scale.
insights.quote: data centers retain the right to wait for a firm connection wherever they choose to site, with non-firm access merely an option
insights.locator: Even while that may be the case

insights.claim: Realizing the grid-positive value will likely require clear commercial or regulatory signals that connecting firm wherever a data center wants is not an option where it would harm the system.
insights.speaker: Tom Brijs
insights.so_what: Track regulators tightening firm-connection rights in congested zones; such reform is the catalyst that unlocks the BTM/non-firm buildout.
insights.quote: connecting firm wherever a data center wants is simply not an alternative where it would negatively impact the system
insights.locator: Even while that may be the case

insights.claim: The approach is not universally feasible and requires changing siting, connection, and operating practices plus today's rules on BTM usage and permitting.
insights.speaker: Tom Brijs
insights.so_what: Adoption is gated by permitting reform and local feasibility; the model applies selectively, not everywhere.
insights.quote: it will not be feasible everywhere. But where it is, grid-positive data centers should be the goal.
insights.locator: None of this is a quick fix

insights.claim: BCG built a model that jointly optimizes load flexibility, BTM assets, and firm-versus-non-firm grid access to find the least-cost way to meet data-center demand over a 2030-2035 horizon in Northwest Europe.
insights.speaker: Tom Brijs
insights.so_what: A stakeholder-by-stakeholder cost-optimization model signals BCG advising utilities, hyperscalers, and regulators on optimal connection strategy through 2035.
insights.quote: BCG has built a model that jointly optimizes load flexibility, BTM assets, and firm versus non-firm grid access to find the least-cost way to meet data-center demand
insights.locator: To quantify this, BCG has built a model
